{{Short description|Antisymmetric permutation object acting on tensors}}{{Distinguish|Levi-Civita connection}}
{{hatnote|See [[Ricci calculus]], [[Einstein notation]], and [[Raising and lowering indices]] for the [[index notation]] used in the article.}}

In [[mathematics]], particularly in [[linear algebra]], [[tensor analysis]], and [[differential geometry]], the '''Levi-Civita symbol''' or '''Levi-Civita epsilon''' represents a collection of numbers defined from the [[parity of a permutation|sign of a permutation]] of the [[natural number]]s {{math|1, 2, ..., ''n''}}, for some positive integer {{mvar|n}}. It is named after the Italian mathematician and physicist [[Tullio Levi-Civita]]. Other names include the '''[[permutation]] symbol''', '''antisymmetric symbol''', or '''alternating symbol''', which refer to its [[antisymmetric tensor|antisymmetric]] property and definition in terms of permutations.

The standard letters to denote the Levi-Civita symbol are the Greek lower case [[epsilon]] {{mvar|ε}} or {{mvar|ϵ}}, or less commonly the Latin lower case {{mvar|e}}. Index notation allows one to display permutations in a way compatible with tensor analysis: <math display="block">\varepsilon_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_n}</math> where ''each'' index {{math|''i''<sub>1</sub>, ''i''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''i''<sub>''n''</sub>}} takes values {{math|1, 2, ..., ''n''}}. There are {{math|''n''<sup>''n''</sup>}} indexed values of {{math|''ε''<sub>''i''<sub>1</sub>''i''<sub>2</sub>...''i<sub>n</sub>''</sub>}}, which can be arranged into an {{mvar|n}}-dimensional array. The key defining property of the symbol is ''total antisymmetry'' in the indices. When any two indices are interchanged, equal or not, the symbol is negated: <math display="block">\varepsilon_{\dots i_p \dots i_q \dots } = -\varepsilon_{\dots i_q \dots i_p \dots } .</math>

If any two indices are equal, the symbol is zero. When all indices are unequal, we have: <math display="block">\varepsilon_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_n} = (-1)^p \varepsilon_{1 \, 2 \, \dots n} ,</math> where {{mvar|p}} (called the parity of the permutation) is the number of pairwise interchanges of indices necessary to unscramble {{math|''i''<sub>1</sub>, ''i''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''i''<sub>''n''</sub>}} into the order {{math|1, 2, ..., ''n''}}, and the factor {{math|(−1)<sup>''p''</sup>}} is called the [[Parity of a permutation|sign, or signature]] of the permutation. The value {{math|''ε''<sub>1 2 ... ''n''</sub>}} must be defined, else the particular values of the symbol for all permutations are indeterminate. Most authors choose {{math|1=''ε''<sub>1 2 ... ''n''</sub> = +1}}, which means the Levi-Civita symbol equals the sign of a permutation when the indices are all unequal. This choice is used throughout this article.

The term "{{mvar|n}}-dimensional Levi-Civita symbol" refers to the fact that the number of indices on the symbol {{mvar|n}} matches the [[dimension]]ality of the [[vector space]] in question, which may be [[Euclidean space|Euclidean]] or [[non-Euclidean space|non-Euclidean]], for example, <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> or [[Minkowski space]]. The values of the Levi-Civita symbol are independent of any [[metric tensor]] and [[coordinate system]]. Also, the specific term "symbol" emphasizes that it is not a [[tensor]] because of how it transforms between coordinate systems; however it can be interpreted as a [[tensor density]].

The Levi-Civita symbol allows the [[determinant]] of a square matrix, and the [[cross product]] of two vectors in three-dimensional Euclidean space, to be expressed in [[Einstein notation|Einstein index notation]].

==Definition==
The Levi-Civita symbol is most often used in three and four dimensions, and to some extent in two dimensions, so these are given here before defining the general case.

===Two dimensions===
In [[two dimensions]], the Levi-Civita symbol is defined by:
<math display="block"> \varepsilon_{ij} =
  \begin{cases}
   +1       & \text{if } (i, j) = (1, 2) \\
   -1       & \text{if } (i, j) = (2, 1) \\
    \;\;\,0 & \text{if } i = j
  \end{cases}
</math>
The values can be arranged into a 2&nbsp;×&nbsp;2 [[antisymmetric matrix]]:
<math display="block">\begin{pmatrix}
    \varepsilon_{11} & \varepsilon_{12} \\
    \varepsilon_{21} & \varepsilon_{22}
  \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
     0 & 1 \\
    -1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}</math>

Use of the two-dimensional symbol is common in condensed matter, and in certain specialized high-energy topics like [[supersymmetry]]<ref>{{cite book|title=Supersymmetry| first=P.|last=Labelle| series=Demystified| publisher=McGraw-Hill| pages=57–58| year=2010| isbn=978-0-07-163641-4}}</ref> and [[twistor theory]],<ref>{{cite web| access-date=2013-09-03| title=Twistor Primer| first=F.| last=Hadrovich| url=http://users.ox.ac.uk/~tweb/00004/index.shtml| archive-date=2015-04-01| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150401000417/http://users.ox.ac.uk/~tweb/00004/index.shtml| url-status=dead}}</ref> where it appears in the context of 2-[[spinors]].

===Three dimensions===
[[File:Permutation indices 3d numerical.svg|thumb|210px|For the indices {{math|(''i'', ''j'', ''k'')}} in {{math|''ε''<sub>''ijk''</sub>}}, the values {{math|1, 2, 3}} occurring in the {{color box|orange}} cyclic order {{math|(1, 2, 3)}} correspond to {{math|1=''ε'' = +1}}, while occurring in the {{color box|red}} reverse cyclic order correspond to {{math|1=''ε'' = −1}}, otherwise {{math|1=''ε'' = 0}}.]]
In [[three dimensions]], the Levi-Civita symbol is defined by:<ref name="Tyldesley">{{cite book| first=J.&nbsp;R. |last=Tyldesley| title=An introduction to Tensor Analysis: For Engineers and Applied Scientists| publisher=Longman| year=1973 | isbn=0-582-44355-5}}</ref>
<math display="block"> \varepsilon_{ijk} = \begin{cases}
         +1 & \text{if } (i,j,k) \text{ is } (1,2,3), (2,3,1), \text{ or } (3,1,2), \\
         -1 & \text{if } (i,j,k) \text{ is } (3,2,1), (1,3,2), \text{ or } (2,1,3), \\
    \;\;\,0 & \text{if } i = j, \text{ or } j = k, \text{ or } k = i
\end{cases}</math>

That is, {{math|''ε''<sub>''ijk''</sub>}} is {{math|1}} if {{math|(''i'', ''j'', ''k'')}} is an [[even and odd permutations|even permutation]] of {{math|(1, 2, 3)}}, {{math|−1}} if it is an [[odd permutation]], and 0 if any index is repeated. In three dimensions only, the [[cyclic permutation]]s of {{math|(1, 2, 3)}} are all even permutations, similarly the [[anticyclic permutation]]s are all odd permutations. This means in 3d it is sufficient to take cyclic or anticyclic permutations of {{math|(1, 2, 3)}} and easily obtain all the even or odd permutations.

Analogous to 2-dimensional matrices, the values of the 3-dimensional Levi-Civita symbol can be arranged into a {{nowrap|3 × 3 × 3}} array:
:[[File:Epsilontensor.svg|200px]]
where {{mvar|i}} is the depth ({{color|blue|blue}}: {{math|1=''i'' = 1}}; {{color|red|red}}: {{math|1=''i'' = 2}}; {{color|green|green}}: {{math|1=''i'' = 3}}), {{mvar|j}} is the row and {{mvar|k}} is the column.

Some examples:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \varepsilon_{\color{BrickRed}{1}  \color{Violet}{3}  \color{Orange}{2}} = -\varepsilon_{\color{BrickRed}{1}  \color{Orange}{2} \color{Violet}{3}} &= - 1 \\
  \varepsilon_{  \color{Violet}{3} \color{BrickRed}{1}  \color{Orange}{2}} = -\varepsilon_{  \color{Orange}{2} \color{BrickRed}{1} \color{Violet}{3}} &= -(-\varepsilon_{\color{BrickRed}{1} \color{Orange}{2} \color{Violet}{3}}) = 1 \\
  \varepsilon_{  \color{Orange}{2}  \color{Violet}{3} \color{BrickRed}{1}} = -\varepsilon_{\color{BrickRed}{1} \color{Violet}{3} \color{Orange}{2}} &= -(-\varepsilon_{\color{BrickRed}{1} \color{Orange}{2} \color{Violet}{3}}) = 1 \\
  \varepsilon_{  \color{Orange}{2}  \color{Violet}{3}  \color{Orange}{2}} = -\varepsilon_{  \color{Orange}{2}  \color{Violet}{3} \color{Orange}{2}} &= 0
\end{align}</math>

===Four dimensions===
In [[Four-dimensional space|four dimensions]], the Levi-Civita symbol is defined by:
<math display="block">\varepsilon_{ijkl} = \begin{cases}
+1 & \text{if }(i,j,k,l) \text{ is an even permutation of } (1,2,3,4) \\
-1 & \text{if }(i,j,k,l) \text{ is an odd permutation of } (1,2,3,4) \\
\;\;\,0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}</math>

These values can be arranged into a {{nowrap|4 × 4 × 4 × 4}} array, although in 4 dimensions and higher this is difficult to draw.

Some examples:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\varepsilon_{\color{BrickRed}{1} \color{RedViolet}{4}\color{Violet}{3} \color{Orange}{\color{Orange}{2}}} = -\varepsilon_{\color{BrickRed}{1} \color{Orange}{\color{Orange}{2}} \color{Violet}{3} \color{RedViolet}{4}} &= - 1\\
\varepsilon_{\color{Orange}{\color{Orange}{2}} \color{BrickRed}{1} \color{Violet}{3} \color{RedViolet}{4}} = -\varepsilon_{\color{BrickRed}{1} \color{Orange}{\color{Orange}{2}} \color{Violet}{3} \color{RedViolet}{4}} &= -1\\
\varepsilon_{\color{RedViolet}{4} \color{Violet}{3} \color{Orange}{\color{Orange}{2}} \color{BrickRed}{1}} = -\varepsilon_{\color{BrickRed}{1} \color{Violet}{3} \color{Orange}{\color{Orange}{2}} \color{RedViolet}{4}} &= -(-\varepsilon_{\color{BrickRed}{1} \color{Orange}{\color{Orange}{2}} \color{Violet}{3} \color{RedViolet}{4}}) = 1\\
\varepsilon_{\color{Violet}{3} \color{Orange}{\color{Orange}{2}} \color{RedViolet}{4} \color{Violet}{3}} = -\varepsilon_{\color{Violet}{3} \color{Orange}{\color{Orange}{2}} \color{RedViolet}{4}\color{Violet}{3}} &= 0
\end{align}</math>

===Generalization to ''n'' dimensions===
More generally, in [[n-dimensional space|{{math|''n''}} dimensions]], the Levi-Civita symbol is defined by:<ref name="Kay">{{cite book| first=D.&nbsp;C. |last=Kay| title=Tensor Calculus| series=Schaum's Outlines |publisher=McGraw Hill | year=1988 | isbn=0-07-033484-6}}</ref>
<math display="block">\varepsilon_{a_1 a_2 a_3 \ldots a_n} = \begin{cases}
         +1 & \text{if }(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots, a_n) \text{ is an even permutation of } (1, 2, 3, \dots, n) \\
         -1 & \text{if }(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots, a_n) \text{ is an odd permutation of } (1, 2, 3, \dots, n) \\
    \;\;\,0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}</math>

Thus, it is the [[even and odd permutations|sign of the permutation]] in the case of a permutation, and zero otherwise.

Using the [[Multiplication#Capital pi notation|capital pi notation]] {{math|Π}} for ordinary multiplication of numbers, an explicit expression for the symbol is:{{cn|date=July 2021}}
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \varepsilon_{a_1 a_2 a_3 \ldots a_n}
    & = \prod_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} \sgn (a_j - a_i) \\
    & = \sgn(a_2 - a_1) \sgn(a_3 - a_1) \dotsm \sgn(a_n - a_1) \sgn(a_3 - a_2) \sgn(a_4 - a_2) \dotsm \sgn(a_n - a_2) \dotsm \sgn(a_n - a_{n-1})
\end{align}</math>
where the [[signum function]] (denoted {{math|sgn}}) returns the sign of its argument while discarding the [[absolute value]] if nonzero. The formula is valid for all index values, and for any {{mvar|n}} (when {{math|1=''n'' = 0}} or {{math|1=''n'' = 1}}, this is the [[empty product]]). However, computing the formula above naively has a [[time complexity]] of {{math|O(''n''<sup>2</sup>)}}, whereas the sign can be computed from the parity of the permutation from its [[permutation#Cycle notation|disjoint cycles]] in only {{math|O(''n'' log(''n''))}} cost.

==Properties==
A tensor whose components in an [[orthonormal basis]] are given by the Levi-Civita symbol (a tensor of [[Covariance and contravariance of vectors|covariant]] rank {{mvar|n}}) is sometimes called a '''permutation tensor'''.

Under the ordinary transformation rules for tensors the Levi-Civita symbol is unchanged under pure rotations, consistent with that it is (by definition) the same in all coordinate systems related by orthogonal transformations. However, the Levi-Civita symbol is a [[pseudotensor]] because under an [[Orthogonal matrix|orthogonal transformation]] of [[jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian determinant]] −1, for example, a [[Reflection (mathematics)|reflection]] in an odd number of dimensions, it ''should'' acquire a minus sign if it were a tensor. As it does not change at all, the Levi-Civita symbol is, by definition, a pseudotensor.

As the Levi-Civita symbol is a pseudotensor, the result of taking a cross product is a [[pseudovector]], not a vector.<ref name="Riley et al">{{cite book|first1=K.&nbsp;F. |last1=Riley |first2=M.&nbsp;P.|last2= Hobson |first3=S.&nbsp;J. |last3=Bence | title=Mathematical Methods for Physics and Engineering|url=https://archive.org/details/mathematicalmeth00rile |url-access=registration | publisher=Cambridge University Press| year=2010 | isbn=978-0-521-86153-3}}</ref>

Under a general [[coordinate change]], the components of the permutation tensor are multiplied by the [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]] of the [[transformation matrix]]. This implies that in coordinate frames different from the one in which the tensor was defined, its components can differ from those of the Levi-Civita symbol by an overall factor. If the frame is orthonormal, the factor will be ±1 depending on whether the orientation of the frame is the same or not.<ref name="Riley et al"/>

In index-free tensor notation, the Levi-Civita symbol is replaced by the concept of the [[Hodge dual]].{{cn|date=March 2024}}

Summation symbols can be eliminated by using [[Einstein notation]], where an index repeated between two or more terms indicates summation over that index.  For example,
:<math>\varepsilon_{ijk} \varepsilon^{imn} \equiv \sum_{i=1,2,3} \varepsilon_{ijk} \varepsilon^{imn}</math>.
In the following examples, Einstein notation is used.

===Two dimensions===
In two dimensions, when all {{math|''i'', ''j'', ''m'', ''n''}} each take the values 1 and 2:<ref name="Tyldesley"/>

{{NumBlk|:
 | <math>\varepsilon_{ij} \varepsilon^{mn} = {\delta_i}^m {\delta_j}^n - {\delta_i}^n {\delta_j}^m </math>
 | {{EquationRef|1}}
}}
{{NumBlk|:
 | <math>\varepsilon_{ij} \varepsilon^{in} = {\delta_j}^n </math>
 | {{EquationRef|2}}
}}
{{NumBlk|:
 | <math>\varepsilon_{ij} \varepsilon^{ij} = 2. </math>
 | {{EquationRef|3}}
}}

===Three dimensions===
====Index and symbol values====
In three dimensions, when all {{math|''i'', ''j'', ''k'', ''m'', ''n'', ''p'',''q''}} each take values 1, 2, and 3:<ref name="Tyldesley"/>

{{NumBlk|:
 | <math>\varepsilon_{ijk} \varepsilon^{pqk}=\delta_i{}^{p}\delta_j{}^q - \delta_i{}^q\delta_j{}^p </math>
 | {{EquationRef|4}}
}}
{{NumBlk|:
 | <math>\varepsilon_{jmn} \varepsilon^{imn}=2{\delta_j}^i </math>
 | {{EquationRef|5}}
}}
{{NumBlk|:
 | <math>\varepsilon_{ijk} \varepsilon^{ijk}=6. </math>
 | {{EquationRef|6}}
}}

====Product====
The Levi-Civita symbol is related to the [[Kronecker delta]]. In three dimensions, the relationship is given by the following equations (vertical lines denote the determinant):<ref name="Kay"/>

:<math>\begin{align}
  \varepsilon_{ijk}\varepsilon_{lmn} &= \begin{vmatrix}
    \delta_{il} & \delta_{im} & \delta_{in} \\
    \delta_{jl} & \delta_{jm} & \delta_{jn} \\
    \delta_{kl} & \delta_{km} & \delta_{kn} \\
  \end{vmatrix} \\[6pt]
                                     &= \delta_{il}\left( \delta_{jm}\delta_{kn} - \delta_{jn}\delta_{km}\right) - \delta_{im}\left( \delta_{jl}\delta_{kn} - \delta_{jn}\delta_{kl} \right) + \delta_{in} \left( \delta_{jl}\delta_{km} - \delta_{jm}\delta_{kl} \right). 
\end{align}</math>

A special case of this result occurs when one of the indices is repeated and summed over:

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^3 \varepsilon_{ijk}\varepsilon_{imn} = \delta_{jm}\delta_{kn} - \delta_{jn}\delta_{km}</math>

In Einstein notation, the duplication of the {{mvar|i}} index implies the sum on {{mvar|i}}. The previous is then denoted {{math|''ε<sub>ijk</sub>ε<sub>imn</sub>'' {{=}} ''δ<sub>jm</sub>δ<sub>kn</sub>'' − ''δ<sub>jn</sub>δ<sub>km</sub>''}}.

If two indices are repeated (and summed over), this further reduces to:

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^3 \sum_{j=1}^3 \varepsilon_{ijk}\varepsilon_{ijn} = 2\delta_{kn}</math>

===''n'' dimensions===
====Index and symbol values====
In {{mvar|n}} dimensions, when all {{math|''i''<sub>1</sub>, ...,''i<sub>n</sub>'', ''j''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''j''<sub>''n''</sub>}} take values {{math|1, 2, ..., ''n''}}:{{cn|date=March 2024}}
{{NumBlk|:
 | <math>\varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_n} \varepsilon^{j_1 \dots j_n} = \delta^{j_1 \dots j_n}_{i_1 \dots i_n}</math>
 | {{EquationRef|7}}
}}
{{NumBlk|:
 | <math>\varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_k~i_{k+1} \dots i_n} \varepsilon^{i_1 \dots i_k~j_{k+1} \dots j_n} = \delta_{ i_1 \ldots i_k~i_{k+1} \ldots i_n}^{i_1 \dots i_k~j_{k+1}\ldots j_n} = k!~\delta^{j_{k+1} \dots j_n}_{i_{k+1} \dots i_n} </math>
 | {{EquationRef|8}}
}}
{{NumBlk|:
 | <math>\varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_n}\varepsilon^{i_1 \dots i_n} = n! </math>
 | {{EquationRef|9}}
}}

where the exclamation mark ({{math|!}}) denotes the [[factorial]], and {{math|''δ''{{su|p=''α''...|b=''β''...}}}} is the [[generalized Kronecker delta]]. For any {{mvar|n}}, the property
:<math>\sum_{i, j, k, \dots = 1}^n \varepsilon_{ijk\dots}\varepsilon_{ijk\dots} = n!</math>

follows from the facts that 
* every permutation is either even or odd, 
* {{math|1=(+1)<sup>2</sup> = (−1)<sup>2</sup> = 1}}, and 
* the number of permutations of any {{mvar|n}}-element set number is exactly {{math|''n''!}}.

The particular case of ({{EquationNote|8}}) with <math display="inline">k=n-2</math> is
<math display="block">
\varepsilon_{i_1\dots i_{n-2}jk}\varepsilon^{i_1\dots i_{n-2}lm} = (n-2)!(\delta_j^l\delta_k^m - \delta_j^m\delta^l_k)\,.
</math>

====Product====
In general, for {{mvar|n}} dimensions, one can write the product of two Levi-Civita symbols as:
<math display="block">
\varepsilon_{i_1 i_2 \dots i_n} \varepsilon_{j_1 j_2 \dots j_n} = \begin{vmatrix}
  \delta_{i_1 j_1} & \delta_{i_1 j_2} & \dots  & \delta_{i_1 j_n} \\
  \delta_{i_2 j_1} & \delta_{i_2 j_2} & \dots  & \delta_{i_2 j_n} \\
  \vdots           & \vdots           & \ddots & \vdots \\
  \delta_{i_n j_1} & \delta_{i_n j_2} & \dots  & \delta_{i_n j_n} \\
\end{vmatrix}.
</math>'''Proof:''' Both sides change signs upon switching two indices, so without loss of generality assume <math>i_1 \leq \cdots\leq i_n, j_1 \leq \cdots \leq j_n</math>. If some <math>i_c = i_{c+1}</math> then left side is zero, and right side is also zero since two of its rows are equal. Similarly for <math>j_c = j_{c+1}</math>. Finally, if <math>i_1 < \cdots < i_n, j_1 < \cdots < j_n</math>, then both sides are 1.

===Proofs===
For ({{EquationNote|1}}), both sides are antisymmetric with respect of {{mvar|ij}} and {{mvar|mn}}. We therefore only need to consider the case {{math|''i'' ≠ ''j''}} and {{math|''m'' ≠ ''n''}}. By substitution, we see that the equation holds for {{math|''ε''<sub>12</sub>''ε''<sup>12</sup>}}, that is, for {{math|1=''i'' = ''m'' = 1}} and {{math|1=''j'' = ''n'' = 2}}. (Both sides are then one). Since the equation is antisymmetric in {{mvar|ij}} and {{mvar|mn}}, any set of values for these can be reduced to the above case (which holds). The equation thus holds for all values of {{mvar|ij}} and {{mvar|mn}}.

Using ({{EquationNote|1}}), we have for ({{EquationNote|2}})
:<math> \varepsilon_{ij} \varepsilon^{in} = \delta_i{}^i \delta_j{}^n - \delta_i{}^n \delta_j{}^i = 2 \delta_j{}^n - \delta_j{}^n = \delta_j{}^n \,.</math>

Here we used the [[Einstein summation convention]] with {{mvar|i}} going from 1 to 2. Next, ({{EquationNote|3}}) follows similarly from ({{EquationNote|2}}).

To establish ({{EquationNote|5}}), notice that both sides vanish when {{math|''i'' ≠ ''j''}}. Indeed, if {{math|''i'' ≠ ''j''}}, then one can not choose {{mvar|m}} and {{mvar|n}} such that both permutation symbols on the left are nonzero. Then, with {{math|1=''i'' = ''j''}} fixed, there are only two ways to choose {{mvar|m}} and {{mvar|n}} from the remaining two indices. For any such indices, we have

:<math>\varepsilon_{jmn} \varepsilon^{imn} = \left(\varepsilon^{imn}\right)^2 = 1</math>

(no summation), and the result follows.

Then ({{EquationNote|6}}) follows since {{nowrap|1=3! = 6}} and for any distinct indices {{math|''i'', ''j'', ''k''}} taking values {{nowrap|1, 2, 3}}, we have 
:<math>\varepsilon_{ijk} \varepsilon^{ijk} = 1</math>{{pad|3em}}(no summation, distinct {{math|''i'', ''j'', ''k''}})

==Applications and examples==

===Determinants===
In linear algebra, the [[determinant]] of a {{nowrap|3 × 3}} [[square matrix]] {{math|1='''A''' = [''a<sub>ij</sub>'']}} can be written<ref>{{cite book|edition=4th|first1=S. |last1=Lipcshutz |first2=M. |last2=Lipson | title=Linear Algebra| series=Schaum's Outlines |publisher=McGraw Hill | year=2009 | isbn=978-0-07-154352-1}}</ref>

:<math>\det(\mathbf{A}) = \sum_{i=1}^3 \sum_{j=1}^3 \sum_{k=1}^3 \varepsilon_{ijk} a_{1i} a_{2j} a_{3k}</math>

Similarly the determinant of an {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} matrix {{math|1='''A''' = [''a<sub>ij</sub>'']}} can be written as<ref name="Riley et al"/>

:<math> \det(\mathbf{A}) = \varepsilon_{i_1\dots i_n} a_{1i_1} \dots a_{ni_n},</math>

where each {{mvar|i<sub>r</sub>}} should be summed over {{math|1, ..., ''n''}}, or equivalently:

:<math> \det(\mathbf{A}) = \frac{1}{n!} \varepsilon_{i_1\dots i_n} \varepsilon_{j_1\dots j_n} a_{i_1 j_1} \dots a_{i_n j_n},</math>

where now each {{mvar|i<sub>r</sub>}} and each {{mvar|j<sub>r</sub>}} should be summed over {{math|1, ..., ''n''}}. More generally, we have the identity<ref name="Riley et al"/>

:<math>\sum_{i_1,i_2,\dots}\varepsilon_{i_1\dots i_n} a_{i_1 \, j_1} \dots a_{i_n \, j_n} = \det(\mathbf{A}) \varepsilon_{j_1\dots j_n}</math>

===Vector cross product===
{{Main|cross product}}

====Cross product (two vectors)====
Let <math>(\mathbf{e_1}, \mathbf{e_2}, \mathbf{e_3})</math> a [[Orientation (vector space)|positively oriented]] orthonormal basis of a vector space. If {{math|1=(''a''<sup>1</sup>, ''a''<sup>2</sup>, ''a''<sup>3</sup>)}} and {{math|1=(''b''<sup>1</sup>, ''b''<sup>2</sup>, ''b''<sup>3</sup>)}} are the coordinates of the  [[Vector (geometry)|vector]]s {{math|1='''a'''}} and {{math|1='''b'''}} in this basis, then their cross product can be written as a determinant:<ref name="Riley et al"/>

:<math>
\mathbf{a \times b} =
 \begin{vmatrix} 
 \mathbf{e_1} & \mathbf{e_2} & \mathbf{e_3} \\
 a^1 & a^2 & a^3 \\
 b^1 & b^2 & b^3 \\
 \end{vmatrix}
= \sum_{i=1}^3 \sum_{j=1}^3 \sum_{k=1}^3 \varepsilon_{ijk} \mathbf{e}_i a^j b^k
</math>
hence also using the Levi-Civita symbol, and more simply:
:<math>
(\mathbf{a \times b})^i = \sum_{j=1}^3 \sum_{k=1}^3 \varepsilon_{ijk} a^j b^k.
</math>

In Einstein notation, the summation symbols may be omitted, and the {{mvar|i}}th component of their cross product equals<ref name="Kay"/>

:<math> (\mathbf{a\times b})^i = \varepsilon_{ijk} a^j b^k.</math>

The first component is

:<math>(\mathbf{a\times b})^1 = a^2 b^3-a^3 b^2\,,</math>

then by cyclic permutations of {{nowrap|1, 2, 3}} the others can be derived immediately, without explicitly calculating them from the above formulae:

:<math>\begin{align}
  (\mathbf{a\times b})^2 &= a^3 b^1-a^1 b^3\,, \\
  (\mathbf{a\times b})^3 &= a^1 b^2-a^2 b^1\,.
\end{align}</math>

====Triple scalar product (three vectors)====
From the above expression for the cross product, we have:
:<math>\mathbf{a\times b} = -\mathbf{b\times a}</math>.

If {{math|1='''c''' = (''c''<sup>1</sup>, ''c''<sup>2</sup>, ''c''<sup>3</sup>)}} is a third vector, then the [[triple scalar product]] equals

:<math> \mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b\times c}) = \varepsilon_{ijk} a^i b^j c^k.</math>

From this expression, it can be seen that the triple scalar product is antisymmetric when exchanging any pair of arguments. For example,

:<math>\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b\times c})= -\mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{a\times c})</math>.

====Curl (one vector field)====
If {{math|1='''F''' = (''F''<sup>1</sup>, ''F''<sup>2</sup>, ''F''<sup>3</sup>)}} is a vector field defined on some [[open set]] of <math>\mathbb{R}^3</math> as a [[function (mathematics)|function]] of [[position vector|position]] {{math|1='''x''' = (''x''<sup>1</sup>, ''x''<sup>2</sup>, ''x''<sup>3</sup>)}} (using [[Cartesian coordinates]]). Then the {{mvar|i}}th component of the [[curl (mathematics)|curl]] of {{math|'''F'''}} equals<ref name="Kay"/>

:<math> (\nabla \times \mathbf{F})^i(\mathbf{x}) = \varepsilon_{ijk}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^j} F^k(\mathbf{x}),</math>

which follows from the cross product expression above, substituting components of the [[gradient]] vector [[linear operator|operator]] (nabla).

==Tensor density==
In any arbitrary [[curvilinear coordinate system]] and even in the absence of a [[metric tensor|metric]] on the [[manifold]], the Levi-Civita symbol as defined above may be considered to be a [[tensor density]] field in two different ways. It may be regarded as a [[Covariance and contravariance of vectors|contravariant]] tensor density of weight +1 or as a covariant tensor density of weight −1. In ''n'' dimensions using the generalized Kronecker delta,<ref>{{Citation | last1=Murnaghan | first1=F.&nbsp;D. | title=The generalized Kronecker symbol and its application to the theory of determinants | year=1925 | journal=Amer. Math. Monthly  | volume=32 | issue=5 | pages=233–241 | doi=10.2307/2299191| jstor=2299191 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first1=David |last1=Lovelock |first2=Hanno |last2=Rund |title=Tensors, Differential Forms, and Variational Principles |publisher=Courier Dover Publications |year=1989 |isbn=0-486-65840-6 |page=113}}</ref>

:<math>\begin{align}
  \varepsilon^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_n} &= \delta^{\mu_1 \dots \mu_n}_{\,1 \,\dots \,n} \, \\
  \varepsilon_{\nu_1 \dots \nu_n} &= \delta^{\,1 \,\dots \,n}_{\nu_1 \dots \nu_n} \,.
\end{align}</math>

Notice that these are numerically identical. In particular, the sign is the same.

==Levi-Civita tensors==
On a [[pseudo-Riemannian manifold]], one may define a coordinate-invariant covariant tensor field whose coordinate representation agrees with the Levi-Civita symbol wherever the coordinate system is such that the basis of the tangent space is orthonormal with respect to the metric and matches a selected orientation. This tensor should not be confused with the tensor density field mentioned above. The presentation in this section closely follows {{Harvnb|Carroll|2004}}.

The covariant Levi-Civita tensor (also known as the [[Riemannian volume form]]) in any coordinate system that matches the selected orientation is
:<math>E_{a_1\dots a_n} = \sqrt{\left|\det [g_{ab}]\right|}\, \varepsilon_{a_1\dots a_n} \,,</math>

where {{mvar|g<sub>ab</sub>}} is the representation of the metric in that coordinate system. We can similarly consider a contravariant Levi-Civita tensor by raising the indices with the metric as usual,
:<math>E^{a_1\dots a_n} = E_{b_1\dots b_n} \prod_{i=1}^n g^{a_i b_i} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\left|\det [g_{ab}]\right|}} \, \varepsilon^{a_1 \dots a_n},,</math>

but notice that if the [[metric signature]] contains an odd number of negative eigenvalues {{math|''q''}}, then the sign of the components of this tensor differ from the standard Levi-Civita symbol:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Nakahara |first=Mikio |url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.1201/9781315275826/geometry-topology-physics-mikio-nakahara |title=Geometry, Topology and Physics |date=2017-01-31 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-315-27582-6 |edition=2 |location=Boca Raton |doi=10.1201/9781315275826}}</ref>
:<math>E^{a_1\dots a_n} = \frac{ \sgn \left( \det [g_{ab}] \right) }{ \sqrt{ \left| \det [g_{ab}] \right| }} \, \varepsilon^{a_1\dots a_n} ,</math>

where {{math|1=sgn(det[g{{sub|''ab''}}]) = (−1){{sup|''q''}}}}, <math>\varepsilon_{a_1\dots a_n}</math> is the usual Levi-Civita symbol discussed in the rest of this article, and we used the definition of the metric [[determinant]] in the derivation. More explicitly, when the tensor and basis orientation are chosen such that <math display="inline">E_{01\dots n} = +\sqrt{\left|\det [g_{ab}]\right|}</math>, we have that <math>E^{01\dots n} = \frac{\sgn(\det [g_{ab}])}{\sqrt{\left|\det [g_{ab}]\right|}}</math>.

From this we can infer the identity,
:<math>E^{\mu_1\dots\mu_p\alpha_1\dots\alpha_{n-p}}E_{\mu_1\dots\mu_p\beta_1\dots\beta_{n-p}} = (-1)^q p!\delta^{\alpha_1\dots\alpha_{n-p}}_{\beta_1\dots\beta_{n-p}} \,,</math>
where
:<math>\delta^{\alpha_1 \dots \alpha_{n-p}}_{\beta_1 \dots \beta_{n-p}} = (n-p)! \delta^{\lbrack \alpha_1}_{\beta_1} \dots \delta^{\alpha_{n-p} \rbrack}_{\beta_{n-p}}</math>
is the generalized Kronecker delta.

===Example: Minkowski space===
In Minkowski space (the four-dimensional [[spacetime]] of [[special relativity]]), the covariant Levi-Civita tensor is
:<math>E_{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} = \pm \sqrt{ \left| \det [g_{\mu \nu}] \right| } \, \varepsilon_{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} \,,</math>

where the sign depends on the orientation of the basis.  The contravariant Levi-Civita tensor is
:<math>E^{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} = g^{\alpha \zeta} g^{\beta \eta} g^{\gamma \theta} g^{\delta \iota} E_{\zeta \eta \theta \iota} \,.</math>

The following are examples of the general identity above specialized to Minkowski space (with the negative sign arising from the odd number of negatives in the signature of the metric tensor in either sign convention):
:<math>\begin{align}
        E_{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} E_{\rho \sigma \mu \nu} & = -g_{\alpha \zeta} g_{\beta \eta} g_{\gamma \theta} g_{\delta \iota} \delta^{\zeta \eta \theta \iota}_{\rho \sigma \mu \nu} \\
        E^{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} E^{\rho \sigma \mu \nu} & = -g^{\alpha \zeta} g^{\beta \eta} g^{\gamma \theta} g^{\delta \iota} \delta^{\rho \sigma \mu \nu}_{\zeta \eta \theta \iota} \\
   E^{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} E_{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} & = - 24 \\
   E^{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} E_{\rho \beta \gamma \delta} & = - 6 \delta^{\alpha}_{\rho} \\
   E^{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} E_{\rho \sigma \gamma \delta} & = - \delta^{\alpha \beta}_{\rho \sigma} \\
   E^{\alpha \beta \gamma \delta} E_{\rho \sigma \theta \delta} & = - \delta^{\alpha \beta \gamma}_{\rho \sigma \theta} \,.
\end{align}</math>
